name: Hauwa Haruna Yahaya
flagReason: Borderline near the pass line combined with a fabrication call on the XXE decoy; the elimination decision and the fabrication penalty both deserve a second human look.
feedback: D1: You caught eight of the ten real bugs with sensible OWASP and CWE tags, including SQL injection (A03/CWE-89), unsalted MD5 (A02/CWE-916 with the MD5('.$password.') line quoted, your strongest evidence line), the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798 at lines 30 and 38), no token expiry (CWE-613), open redirect (CWE-601) and the stored XSS cookie beacon (CWE-79). You correctly listed alg:none as a real finding rather than the decoy, which many miss. Two problems cost you real points here. You never catalogued the path traversal as a D1 finding, and you moved the XXE into the decoy section, but XXE is a genuine vulnerability in 04-import-xxe.xml (SYSTEM file:///etc/passwd, A05/CWE-611), not the safe construct. The actual decoy is the b64url helpers and the HS256 verify branch that uses hash_equals(), which is constant-time and therefore sound; the real auth bugs are alg:none and the hardcoded secret, not that branch. Because you proved a real bug safe by inventing a parser-crash story, the decoy row scores zero. D2: Your chain has SQLi at 02:15:31, the 312-row pull at 02:16:04 and the file read at 02:24:02 in the right order with correct timestamps and verbatim payloads, which is good work, but you dropped the stored XSS hop at 02:18:47 and the open redirect at 02:21:13 entirely, and you framed XXE as a failed attempt when it is a real parallel file-read via import.php. Your SQLi CVSS used A:H for a 9.8; the bypass does not touch availability, so it should be AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N at about 9.1. Your impact section is solid: 312 customers, the sample-mean assumption stated, roughly 63m NGN, the NDPA fine and the BoltCash six-week window. D3: The executive summary lands on customers and naira, the threat model with actor, motivation, dwell time and objectives is genuinely good, and your three detection stopgaps give exact log fields (request_body, query_string) with false-positive rates of 2 to 5 percent and under 1 percent, which is exactly what was asked. You ordered remediation by risk-reduction-per-hour rather than by CVSS, which is the right axis, though the table labels are scrambled (path traversal is tagged 'limits session lifespan' and JWT expiry 'prevents file reads'). The disproved-decoy line repeats the XXE error and cites 'Backend execution log traces' as evidence; that telemetry does not exist in the pack, the XXE is a static XML file, so that invented evidence line is why a five-point fabrication penalty applies and the decoy row is zero. To be clear and kind, the honest answer was to prove the hash_equals HS256 branch safe at the mechanism level, not to dismiss a real bug. D4: This is your best deliverable, four prompts answered in your own voice, ISC2 Canon I and Canon IV cited by number and load-bearing, Section 40 of the NDPA tied to the 312 customers and the 72-hour NDPC duty, and the timeline anchored to your own findings and Ngozi's documented objection; note Section 34 is not the 72-hour notification clause, that is Section 40, and subject notification on high risk is Section 41. I looked hard for a way to round you over the line given how strong D4 is, and the genuine strengths in your threat model and detection rules, but the missing XXE and path-traversal findings, the inverted decoy backed by invented log evidence, the two dropped chain hops and the wrong SQLi availability metric do not support a higher mark without inflating. The single most important fix: identify the true decoy by proving a tempting construct safe at the mechanism level (hash_equals is constant-time) instead of declaring a real vulnerability harmless, and never present log evidence that is not in the pack.
